questions.stem: The DOUBLE-HELIX structure of DNA was proposed in 1953 by:

options.option_text: Watson and Crick (with key X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins)

questions.explanation: James Watson + Francis Crick — proposed the double-helix model in Nature, April 1953. Used the X-ray crystallography 'Photo 51' produced by Rosalind Franklin (in Maurice Wilkins's lab at King's College London). Nobel 1962 — Watson, Crick, Wilkins; Franklin had passed away in 1958 (ovarian cancer); Nobel rules don't allow posthumous awards. Earlier — Erwin Chargaff (1950) showed A = T, G = C ('Chargaff's rules'). Frederick Griffith (1928) — bacterial transformation; Avery-MacLeod-McCarty (1944) — DNA, not protein, is the genetic material. Hershey-Chase (1952) — phage experiment confirmed DNA as the hereditary molecule.

questions.stem: In DNA, ADENINE (A) pairs with which base via two hydrogen bonds?

options.option_text: Thymine (T) — in RNA, A pairs with Uracil (U)

questions.explanation: DNA base pairing rule (Chargaff): A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds). Purines (A, G) — double-ring structure; pyrimidines (C, T, U) — single-ring. Pairing always purine-pyrimidine (matching the double-helix's uniform width). RNA — uses URACIL instead of thymine; A pairs with U. The ratios A:T and G:C are always 1:1 in any DNA sample (Chargaff's rule). Higher G+C content → higher melting temperature (more H-bonds → more stable). Bacteria genomes vary widely (e.g., Streptomyces ~70% G+C, Plasmodium ~20%).

questions.stem: Of the three types of RNA, the one that CARRIES amino acids to the ribosome during protein synthesis is:
questions.explanation: Three main types of RNA in protein synthesis: (1) mRNA (messenger) — carries the genetic code from DNA (nucleus) to the ribosome (cytoplasm); single-stranded, has codons. (2) tRNA (transfer) — clover-leaf-shaped; ANTICODON loop reads the mRNA codon; carries the corresponding amino acid attached to its 3' CCA end. (3) rRNA (ribosomal) — structural + catalytic component of the ribosome (the actual peptidyl transferase enzyme is RNA-based — a ribozyme). Other RNAs: snRNA (in spliceosome — splicing), miRNA (microRNA — gene regulation), siRNA (small interfering RNA — RNAi technology, basis of Nobel 2024 to Victor Ambros & Gary Ruvkun for miRNA discovery).

questions.stem: The genetic code is read in groups of how many nucleotides at a time (each group coding for one amino acid)?
questions.explanation: Codon — triplet of three nucleotides. With 4 bases, possible triplets = 4³ = 64. 61 code for the 20 standard amino acids (genetic code is DEGENERATE — multiple codons can code for the same amino acid). 3 are STOP codons — UAA, UAG, UGA (no amino acid; signal end of translation). START codon — AUG (codes for methionine; also marks where translation begins). The genetic code is nearly universal across all life — strong evidence of common ancestry. Slight exceptions in mitochondrial code, some ciliates, some bacteria. Khorana, Nirenberg, Holley — Nobel 1968 for cracking the code.

questions.stem: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) — invented by Kary Mullis (Nobel 1993) — is a technique used for:

options.option_text: Amplifying specific DNA sequences exponentially in vitro (used in COVID testing, forensics, paternity tests)

questions.explanation: PCR — invented 1983 by Kary Mullis (Nobel Chemistry 1993). Cycles: (1) DENATURATION — heat to ~95°C, DNA strands separate; (2) ANNEALING — cool to ~55°C, primers bind to target sequences; (3) EXTENSION — heat to ~72°C, Taq polymerase (heat-stable, from Thermus aquaticus, Yellowstone hot-spring bacterium) synthesises new strands. Each cycle DOUBLES the target — 30 cycles → ~10⁹-fold amplification. Applications: COVID-19 RT-PCR (real-time PCR for RNA viruses), DNA fingerprinting (forensics), paternity testing, ancient-DNA analysis, prenatal diagnostics. Real-time / qPCR — allows quantification by tracking fluorescence after each cycle.

questions.stem: A mutation that changes a single base pair in DNA — and may change a single amino acid in the resulting protein — is called a:

options.option_text: Point mutation (specifically, a missense mutation if it changes the amino acid)

questions.explanation: POINT MUTATION — single nucleotide substitution (one base replaced by another). Subtypes: (1) SILENT — codon changes but encodes the same amino acid (genetic code redundancy); (2) MISSENSE — encodes a different amino acid (e.g., sickle cell disease — single A→T in beta-haemoglobin gene → glutamate becomes valine); (3) NONSENSE — creates a premature STOP codon → truncated protein (e.g., some cystic fibrosis cases). FRAMESHIFT — insertion/deletion (indel) of a non-multiple-of-3 number of bases → reading frame shifts → all downstream amino acids change. Larger-scale: CHROMOSOMAL aberrations (deletion, duplication, inversion, translocation); ANEUPLOIDY (extra/missing chromosome — Down syndrome trisomy 21, Turner XO, Klinefelter XXY).

questions.stem: The Human Genome Project — completed in 2003 — revealed that humans have approximately how many protein-coding genes?
questions.explanation: Human Genome Project (HGP) — international 1990-2003 effort; first draft 2001, complete in 2003 (50th anniversary of the double helix). 3 billion base pairs sequenced. Surprise: only ~20,000-25,000 protein-coding genes — fewer than the fruit fly (~14,000) only by a small factor; most of the genome (~98%) is non-coding (regulatory, repetitive, transposons, ncRNA). Cost: ~$3 billion (1990s); today, a human genome can be sequenced for under $1,000 (Illumina). Telomere-to-telomere (T2T) consortium completed the FINAL ~8% of unsolved heterochromatic regions in 2022. Indian initiative — IndiGen project (CSIR, ~10,000 genomes, completed 2020).
